title: Motion, Graphs & Measurement
description: Measuring length, time and volume; average speed; distance-time and speed-time graphs; acceleration, free fall, scalars and vectors, and terminal velocity for IGCSE Physics 0625.

notes.heading: Measuring Length, Time and Volume
notes.body:
0625 expects you to describe HOW a measurement is made, not just quote a value.

📌 Definitions and instruments
• **Length**: measure with a rule (short lengths) or a measuring tape (longer lengths). Read the scale at eye level to avoid parallax error.
• **Volume of a liquid**: pour into a measuring cylinder and read the BOTTOM of the meniscus at eye level.
• **Volume of an irregular solid**: the displacement method — part-fill a measuring cylinder with water, record the level, lower the object in on a thread, record the new level. The rise in level equals the object's volume.
• **Time intervals**: use a stopwatch. For a short repeated event such as a pendulum swing, time MANY swings and divide.

💡 Worked Example
A stopwatch records $25$ s for $20$ complete swings of a pendulum. The period (time for one swing) is $T = \dfrac{25}{20} = 1.25$ s — far more accurate than timing one swing, because the reaction-time error is shared between all 20 swings.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Timing a single swing. Human reaction time (~$0.2$ s) is a large fraction of one swing but a small fraction of twenty.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Check for a zero error before using any scale.
• Volume of displaced water = volume of the submerged object.
• More repetitions + division = smaller percentage error in timing.

notes.heading: Average Speed: v = s/t
notes.body:
📌 Definition
$$\text{average speed} = \dfrac{\text{total distance travelled}}{\text{total time taken}} \qquad v = \dfrac{s}{t}$$
Units: metres per second (m/s) when distance is in metres and time in seconds. This is the syllabus phrase 'recall and use' — you must be able to rearrange it: $s = vt$ and $t = \dfrac{s}{v}$.

🔑 How it works
'Average' matters: a journey may include stops and changes of speed, but the average uses only the TOTAL distance and TOTAL time, including any time spent stopped.

💡 Worked Example
A car travels $150$ m in $10$ s: $v = \dfrac{150}{10} = 15$ m/s.
A train covers $120$ m at $30$ m/s: $t = \dfrac{120}{30} = 4.0$ s.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing units. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by $3.6$: $72$ km/h $= \dfrac{72}{3.6} = 20$ m/s. Convert BEFORE substituting into $v = s/t$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Speed is how fast; it says nothing about direction.
• A speedometer shows instantaneous speed; the exam almost always wants average speed.

notes.heading: Distance-Time Graphs
notes.body:
A distance-time graph plots distance travelled (y-axis) against time (x-axis). The SHAPE of the line tells you the motion.

🔑 How to read it
• **Straight line sloping up**: constant speed. Steeper line = greater speed.
• **Horizontal line**: the object is stationary (distance is not changing).
• **Curved line**: the speed is changing — curving steeper means speeding up, flattening means slowing down.

📌 The gradient IS the speed
$$\text{speed} = \text{gradient} = \dfrac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}$$
To calculate a gradient, pick two points on the line that are FAR APART and sit on grid crossings, then divide the rise by the run.

💡 Worked Example
A straight line passes through $(0, 0)$ and $(10\text{ s}, 60\text{ m})$: speed $= \dfrac{60}{10} = 6$ m/s.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading the VALUE off the y-axis instead of computing the GRADIENT. At $t = 10$ s the distance is $60$ m, but the speed is $6$ m/s.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Distance-time graphs can never slope downwards — distance travelled cannot decrease.
• A return journey needs a DISPLACEMENT-time graph, which can go negative.

notes.heading: Speed-Time Graphs
notes.body:
A speed-time graph plots speed (y-axis) against time (x-axis). It carries MORE information than a distance-time graph.

🔑 How to read it
• **Straight line sloping up**: constant acceleration. Steeper = greater acceleration.
• **Horizontal line**: constant speed (zero acceleration).
• **Straight line sloping down**: constant deceleration (negative acceleration).

📌 Two exam skills
1. The **gradient** is the acceleration (Extended tier): $a = \dfrac{\text{change in speed}}{\text{time taken}}$.
2. The **area under the line** is the distance travelled. Split the area into rectangles and triangles: rectangle area $= \text{base} \times \text{height}$, triangle area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.

💡 Worked Example
A cyclist speeds up from $0$ to $10$ m/s in $5$ s, then holds $10$ m/s for $10$ s. Distance $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10 + 10 \times 10 = 25 + 100 = 125$ m.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using 'distance = speed x time' for the speeding-up section. That formula needs CONSTANT speed; during acceleration you must use the triangle area (or the average speed, which is half the final speed when starting from rest).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Gradient of a speed-time graph = acceleration; area = distance.
• A line ON the time axis means the object is at rest.

illustration.alt: Two exam-style motion graphs: a distance-time graph showing that gradient equals speed, and a speed-time graph showing that gradient equals acceleration and the shaded area equals distance travelled.
illustration.caption: Distance-time: gradient = speed. Speed-time: gradient = acceleration, area = distance.

notes.heading: Acceleration and Free Fall
notes.body:
📌 Definition (Extended tier)
Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time:
$$a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$$
where $u$ is the initial velocity, $v$ the final velocity and $t$ the time taken. Unit: metres per second squared (m/s$^2$). A negative value is a deceleration.

🔑 Free fall
Any object falling near the Earth's surface, with air resistance ignored, accelerates downwards at the **acceleration of free fall** $g \approx 9.8$ m/s$^2$. This value is the same for every object, heavy or light — a hammer and a feather fall together on the Moon.

💡 Worked Example
A stone is dropped from rest. After $3.0$ s its speed is $v = u + at = 0 + 9.8 \times 3.0 = 29.4$ m/s downwards.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing acceleration in m/s. An acceleration of $9.8$ m/s$^2$ means the speed GAINS $9.8$ m/s every second.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $g \approx 9.8$ m/s$^2$ — quote this value in the exam.
• Deceleration is just acceleration with a negative sign.
• In free fall the speed-time graph is a straight line of gradient $g$ (until air resistance matters).

notes.heading: Scalars and Vectors
notes.body:
📌 Definitions (Extended tier)
A **scalar** has magnitude (size) only: distance, speed, mass, time, energy, temperature.
A **vector** has magnitude AND direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum.

🔑 How it works
Velocity is speed in a stated direction, so an object moving in a circle at constant speed still has a changing velocity. Distance measures the total path; displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish in a stated direction — walk once around a 400 m track and your distance is $400$ m but your displacement is $0$ m.

💡 Worked Example — combining perpendicular vectors
Two forces act at right angles on a boat: $3$ N east and $4$ N north. The resultant is found by drawing the vectors head-to-tail and completing the right-angled triangle:
$$R = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ N}$$
The same scale-drawing or Pythagoras method gives the resultant of any two perpendicular vectors.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Adding vectors as if they were scalars: $3$ N + $4$ N is NOT $7$ N when the forces are perpendicular. $7$ N would only be correct if they acted along the same line in the same direction.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Speed: scalar. Velocity: vector. Distance: scalar. Displacement: vector.
• At right angles, use Pythagoras for the resultant.

notes.heading: Terminal Velocity
notes.body:
Falling through air is a competition between weight (constant) and air resistance (grows with speed). Describing this motion on a speed-time graph is a classic Extended-tier question.

🔑 The skydiver story — stage by stage
1. **Just after leaving the aircraft**: weight exceeds air resistance, so there is a downward resultant force and the skydiver accelerates at nearly $g$.
2. **Speed builds**: air resistance increases with speed, so the resultant force (and the acceleration) DECREASES. The speed-time line curves and flattens.
3. **Terminal velocity**: air resistance has grown until it EQUALS the weight. The resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero, and the skydiver falls at a constant speed — the terminal velocity.
4. **Parachute opens**: the large area makes air resistance suddenly greater than weight, so the skydiver decelerates until a new, LOWER terminal velocity is reached.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Terminal velocity means ZERO resultant force, not zero force: weight and drag are balanced.
• A larger surface area (parachute) or a smaller weight gives a lower terminal velocity.
• On the speed-time graph, terminal velocity is the horizontal section.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying the skydiver 'stops accelerating because the forces disappear'. The forces do not disappear — they balance.

flashcards.definition: Total distance travelled divided by total time taken: v = s/t. Units m/s.
flashcards.example: 150 m in 10 s gives an average speed of 15 m/s.

flashcards.definition: Volume of an irregular solid = rise in water level when the object is fully submerged in a measuring cylinder.
flashcards.example: Water rises from 50 cm³ to 72 cm³, so the stone's volume is 22 cm³.

flashcards.definition: Time many complete swings (e.g. 20) with a stopwatch, then divide by the number of swings to get the period.
flashcards.example: 20 swings in 25 s gives a period of 1.25 s.

flashcards.definition: The gradient of a distance-time graph equals the speed. Steeper line = greater speed.
flashcards.example: A line through (0, 0) and (10 s, 60 m) shows a speed of 6 m/s.

flashcards.definition: A horizontal line means the object is stationary — distance is not changing with time.
flashcards.example: A runner resting at the 100 m mark for 5 s.

flashcards.definition: The gradient of a speed-time graph equals the acceleration (Extended). A downward slope is a deceleration.
flashcards.example: Speed rises 0 to 12 m/s in 6 s: acceleration = 2 m/s².

flashcards.definition: The area under a speed-time graph equals the distance travelled.
flashcards.example: A triangle (25 m) plus a rectangle (100 m) gives 125 m travelled.

flashcards.definition: Change in velocity per unit time: a = (v - u)/t. Unit m/s² (Extended).
flashcards.example: From 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 3 s: a = 12/3 = 4 m/s².

flashcards.definition: The downward acceleration of any object falling near Earth with air resistance ignored: g is approximately 9.8 m/s².
flashcards.example: A dropped stone reaches about 29.4 m/s after 3.0 s.

flashcards.definition: A quantity with magnitude only (Extended). Examples: distance, speed, mass, time, energy, temperature.
flashcards.example: A mass of 5 kg needs no direction.

flashcards.definition: A quantity with magnitude AND direction (Extended). Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight.
flashcards.example: A velocity of 20 m/s due north is a vector; 20 m/s alone is a speed.

flashcards.definition: The constant maximum falling speed reached when air resistance has grown to equal the weight, so the resultant force is zero (Extended).
flashcards.example: A skydiver falls at terminal velocity before the parachute opens; opening it gives a new, lower terminal velocity.

questions.stem: Which equation correctly defines average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, $v = \dfrac{s}{t}$. Multiplying $s \times t$ has no physical meaning here, and $\dfrac{t}{s}$ is the reciprocal — time per metre.

questions.stem: A car travels $150$ m in $10$ s. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed $v = \dfrac{s}{t} = \dfrac{150}{10} = 15\text{ m/s}$. $0.067$ m/s comes from calculating $\dfrac{t}{s}$ — the equation upside down.

questions.stem: A measuring cylinder contains $50\text{ cm}^3$ of water. A stone is lowered in and the level rises to $72\text{ cm}^3$. What is the volume of the stone?
questions.explanation: By the displacement method the stone's volume is the rise in water level: $72 - 50 = 22\text{ cm}^3$. Reading $72\text{ cm}^3$ alone gives the combined volume, not the stone's.

questions.stem: A student times $20$ complete swings of a pendulum as $25$ s. What is the period of one swing?
questions.explanation: The period is the total time divided by the number of swings: $T = \dfrac{25}{20} = 1.25$ s. $0.80$ s comes from dividing the swings by the time — the wrong way round.

questions.stem: On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal section of the line show?
choices: The object is moving at constant speed
The object is returning to its start point
questions.explanation: On a horizontal section the distance is not changing as time passes, so the object is stationary. Constant speed would be a sloping straight line; a distance-time graph can never show a return journey because distance cannot decrease.

questions.stem: A distance-time graph is a straight line from $(0, 0)$ to $(10\text{ s}, 60\text{ m})$. What is the speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is the gradient: $\dfrac{60\text{ m}}{10\text{ s}} = 6\text{ m/s}$. $60$ m/s is the distance value misread as a speed, and $0.17$ m/s is $\dfrac{t}{s}$ inverted.

questions.stem: A cyclist's speed-time graph is a straight line from $0$ to $12\text{ m/s}$ in $6$ s. What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the gradient of a speed-time graph: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{12 - 0}{6} = 2\text{ m/s}^2$. $72\text{ m/s}^2$ comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A speed-time graph rises in a straight line from $0$ to $10\text{ m/s}$ over $5$ s, then stays at $10\text{ m/s}$ for the next $10$ s. What total distance is travelled?
questions.explanation: Distance is the area under the graph: triangle $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10 = 25$ m, plus rectangle $10 \times 10 = 100$ m, total $125$ m. $100$ m forgets the triangle; $25$ m forgets the constant-speed section.

questions.stem: What is the approximate value of the acceleration of free fall near the Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: The acceleration of free fall on Earth is $g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$. $1.6\text{ m/s}^2$ is the Moon's value — a deliberate distractor.

questions.stem: A stone is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed $3.0$ s later? (Take $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.)
questions.explanation: In free fall the speed gains $9.8$ m/s every second: $v = u + gt = 0 + 9.8 \times 3.0 = 29.4\text{ m/s}$. $3.3$ m/s comes from dividing $g$ by the time.

questions.stem: Which of these quantities is a vector?
questions.explanation: A vector has magnitude and direction. Velocity is speed in a stated direction, so it is a vector; speed, distance and mass have magnitude only and are scalars.

questions.stem: A boat experiences a force of $3$ N due east from the current and $4$ N due north from the wind. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
questions.explanation: The forces are perpendicular, so use Pythagoras on the head-to-tail triangle: $R = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ N. $7$ N would only be right if both forces acted along the same line.

questions.stem: On a speed-time graph, a straight line sloping DOWNWARDS shows an object that is:
questions.explanation: A downward slope means the speed is decreasing steadily — a constant deceleration (negative acceleration). A horizontal line, not a sloping one, shows constant speed; a stationary object lies on the time axis.

questions.stem: A train travels at $72$ km/h. What is this speed in m/s?
questions.explanation: Divide km/h by $3.6$: $72 \div 3.6 = 20\text{ m/s}$ (equivalently $72000\text{ m} \div 3600\text{ s}$). $259\text{ m/s}$ comes from multiplying by $3.6$ instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity. Which statement correctly describes the forces on her?
choices: Her weight is zero because she is no longer accelerating
Air resistance is greater than her weight, slowing her down
Air resistance equals her weight, so the resultant force is zero
She is accelerating downwards at $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity air resistance has grown to equal the weight, so the resultant force is zero and the speed is constant. Her weight is unchanged, and acceleration is zero — not $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
